A program that is supposed to decide needs a question to which the only answers are yes or no: Is the temperature in the desired range?
A condition alone does not make anything happen yet; a script still runs line by line from top to bottom (Chapter 1, Section 5.2).
Many tasks consist of repeating the same step until a goal is reached: calculating until a result is accurate enough, waiting until a cup of tea has cooled down.
Often it is clear before the first repetition how many there will be: for each day of a week, for each year of a savings plan.
Controlling loops, nesting them and collecting results
A loop does not have to execute every iteration completely, and it does not always have to run to the end.
Solutions by trying: guess and check, approximation with a tolerance
With conditions and loops, a program can solve equations for which it knows no formula: it tries out candidates and checks each one.
The stepping method feels its way toward the solution with fixed steps and is therefore slow.

In every step, bisection asks only for the sign of f and thereby gains one bit. This section shows a method that also uses the slope of f and thereby roughly doubles the number of significant digits in every step.
Application: the interest rate of an installment loan
Bisection and Newton's method are not made for square roots but for equations that cannot be solved for the unknown.
